title: Helping Your Kids Embrace Your Next Marital Commitment
subtitle: Guiding your children through the journey toward your new marriage
summary: **You have found love again, and your heart is ready to make a new commitment.** But your children may not be ready. They are still grieving their parent, still adjusting to life without them, and now they face another massive change. This journey helps you guide your children through the complex emotions of watching you prepare to marry again, honoring their grief while helping them open their hearts to this new chapter in your family's story.

cover.heroImageDescription: A family silhouette with warm light suggesting hope and togetherness, conveying both the complexity and possibility of blended family formation.

targetOutcomes: Understand your children's perspective on your new relationship
Navigate their grief, loyalty conflicts, and fears
Communicate effectively about your plans to remarry
Help children build relationship with your future spouse
Honor their deceased parent while embracing new family
Prepare your family for the transition ahead

activities.title: Their World Changes Again: Understanding Your Children's Experience
activities.subtitle: Seeing this transition through their eyes
activities.whyThisMatters: Your children have already experienced devastating loss. Now they face another major change. Understanding their perspective is essential to helping them through this transition.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Children experience parental remarriage through the lens of their own grief, development, and attachment needs.

cards.title: They Have Already Lost So Much
cards.text:
**Your children's world was shattered when their parent died.**

**They lost their mother or father.** They lost the family they knew. They lost the future they expected. They lost their sense that the world is safe and predictable.

**And now, just as they are finding their footing in this new reality, the ground shifts again.** You are bringing someone new into the family. Someone who is not their parent. Someone who will share your attention, your home, your life.

**This is not how they imagined things would go.** In their minds, their parent should still be here. The family should still be intact. This new person, no matter how wonderful, represents another deviation from the life they were supposed to have.

**Marcus watched his twelve-year-old daughter's face when he told her he was planning to remarry.** She tried to smile, but he saw the fear behind her eyes. Another change. Another loss of the familiar. Another step away from the family she remembered.

**Your joy about this new relationship is real and valid.** But your children's fear and grief are equally real. Both can coexist.

**"Even youths grow tired and weary, and young men stumble and fall" (Isaiah 40:30|Even youths grow tired and weary, and young men stumble and fall).** Your children are weary. They have been through so much. This transition requires extraordinary gentleness.

cards.title: What They May Be Feeling
cards.text:
**Your children may experience a storm of emotions about your new relationship, many of which they cannot articulate.**

Fear: What will this mean for them? Will they lose more of your attention? Will this person try to replace their parent? Will they have to move, change schools, lose what little stability they have?

**Loyalty conflict: Accepting this new person can feel like betraying their deceased parent.** If they like your partner, does that mean they are forgetting the one who died?

**Anger: This is not fair.** Their parent should not have died. You should not be dating. This person should not be here. The anger may be directed at you, at your partner, at the situation, or at God.

**Sadness: Fresh grief for their parent.** Grief for the family that will never be the same. Sadness that life keeps changing in ways they did not choose.

**Hope: Perhaps hidden under the other emotions, some children also feel hope.** Hope that there might be happiness again. Hope for a complete family. This hope can coexist with fear and grief.

**"The Lord is close to the brokenhearted and saves those who are crushed in spirit" (Psalm 34:18|The Lord is close to the brokenhearted and saves those who are crushed in spirit).** Your children may be brokenhearted about this change even as you are hopeful. God is close to them.

cards.title: Age Makes a Difference
cards.text:
**How your children respond depends partly on their age and development.**

**Young children may adapt more easily in some ways.** They are naturally resilient and may welcome a new parental figure. But they may also have magical thinking, believing their parent will come back, or confusion about family relationships.

**School-age children understand more about death and family.** They may have stronger loyalty conflicts, worry about what friends will think, or resist changes to their routines and home.

**Teenagers often have the hardest time.** They are developmentally pulling away from parents anyway, and a new stepparent complicates that process. They may feel their opinions should carry more weight, resent changes to family dynamics, or worry about practical matters like inheritance or college.

**Adult children are not exempt from struggle.** Even grown children can have strong feelings about a parent remarrying, feeling it dishonors their deceased parent or changes the family in unwelcome ways.

**Elena's three children reacted very differently to her engagement.** Her seven-year-old was excited about having a "new dad." Her fourteen-year-old was furious and refused to discuss it. Her nineteen-year-old was politely distant but clearly uncomfortable. Same news, three completely different responses.

**"Start children off on the way they should go, and even when they are old they will not turn from it" (Proverbs 22:6|new dad.).** Each child needs guidance tailored to where they are.

cards.title: Your Children's Response
cards.text: How have your children responded to your relationship so far? What emotions have you observed?

cards.title: Seeing Through Their Eyes
cards.text:
**Take time to truly see this transition from your children's perspective.**

What losses have they already experienced? What grief are they still carrying?

What fears might they have about this change? Loss of attention, stability, connection to their deceased parent?

What loyalty conflicts might they feel? Does accepting your partner feel like betraying their parent?

How might their age and personality affect their response?

What do they need from you right now? Reassurance, patience, information, space?

**Understanding their experience is the foundation for helping them through this.**
cards.reflection: What do you understand about how your children are experiencing this transition?

cards.title: A Commitment to Their Hearts
cards.text:
**Make a commitment to prioritize your children's hearts through this transition.**

**I will remember that my children have already lost so much.** This change, however positive, is another upheaval in their young lives.

**I will not dismiss their feelings or expect them to share my excitement.** Their emotions are valid, even when inconvenient.

**I will see this transition through their eyes, not just my own.** What feels like a happy new chapter to me may feel like another loss to them.

**I will be patient.** They may need time to adjust that does not match my timeline.

**I will put their wellbeing at the center of how I navigate this.** They did not choose any of this. I will protect them as best I can.

**"Fathers, do not exasperate your children; instead, bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord" (Ephesians 6:4|Fathers, do not exasperate your children; instead, bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord).** I will not exasperate them by ignoring their needs during this transition.

**Write your commitment to your children's hearts.**
cards.reflection: **Write your commitment to prioritizing your children through this transition.**

activities.title: The Loyalty Bind: When Loving Someone New Feels Like Betrayal
activities.subtitle: Helping children navigate conflicting loyalties
activities.whyThisMatters: Children often feel that accepting a stepparent means betraying their deceased parent. Addressing this loyalty conflict directly helps them find freedom.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Children need explicit permission and help to love new family members without feeling disloyal to the deceased.

cards.title: Caught Between Two Loves
cards.text:
**Your child is caught in an impossible bind.**

**They love and miss their deceased parent desperately.** That parent holds a sacred place in their heart, and they feel duty-bound to protect that place.

**But here is this new person who is kind to them, who makes you happy, who might actually be someone they could like.** And liking them feels like treason.

If I enjoy time with this person, am I forgetting my real parent?

If I let them into my heart, am I pushing my parent out?

If I call them a stepparent, does that erase who my actual parent was?

**This is the loyalty bind, and it can paralyze children.** They may push away your partner not because they dislike them, but because getting close feels like betrayal.

**Ten-year-old Jamie liked his mother's boyfriend, Daniel.** Daniel was funny and kind and taught him to fish. But every time Jamie felt warmth toward Daniel, he would think of his dad and feel a wave of guilt. So he started being rude to Daniel, pushing him away to protect his loyalty to his father.

**The bind is real.** Your children need help escaping it.

**"A new command I give you: Love one another" (John 13:34|A new command I give you: Love one another).** Love is not a competition. Loving new people does not diminish love for those who have died.

cards.title: Permission to Love
cards.text:
**Your children need explicit permission to love your new partner without guilt.**

**This permission must come from you, clearly and repeatedly.**

**"It is okay to like [partner's name].** That does not mean you love your [mom/dad] any less."

**"Your [mom/dad] would want you to be happy.** They would not want you to miss out on having another person who cares about you."

**"Loving [partner's name] does not replace your [mom/dad].** Your [mom/dad] will always be your [mom/dad]. There is room in your heart for both."

**"You do not have to choose.** You can love who is here and still love who is gone."

**Children need to hear this multiple times, in different ways, over extended periods.** The guilt does not disappear with one conversation.

**Lisa told her daughter explicitly: "Your dad was my husband and your father, and nothing will ever change that.** Michael is different, not a replacement. You can care about Michael without being disloyal to Dad. Dad would want you to let good people into your life." Her daughter cried with relief. She had been carrying the guilt for months.

**"There is no fear in love. But perfect love drives out fear" (1 John 4:18|Her daughter cried with relief. She had been carrying the guilt for months. **). Help drive out the fear that loving one person means losing another.

cards.title: Your Partner's Role in This
cards.text:
**Your partner can also help release your children from the loyalty bind.**

A wise partner will:

**Honor the deceased parent openly.** Speaking respectfully about them, acknowledging their importance, never competing with their memory.

**Not try to replace them.** Making clear that they are not trying to be Mom or Dad, but rather an additional caring adult.

**Give space for grief.** Understanding that the children's sadness about their parent is not rejection of them.

**Move slowly.** Not forcing closeness but letting relationships develop naturally.

**Carlos, who was engaged to a widow with two children, made a point of saying to her kids: "I know I am not your dad, and I am not trying to be.** Your dad sounds like he was an amazing person. I just want to be someone else who cares about you, if you will let me." The children visibly relaxed. He was not a threat to their father's memory.

**"Do nothing out of selfish ambition or vain conceit. Rather, in humility value others above yourselves" (Philippians 2:3|The children visibly relaxed. He was not a threat to their father's memory. **). A humble partner values the children's needs above their own desire for acceptance.

cards.title: Loyalty Conflicts You See
cards.text: Have you noticed loyalty conflicts in your children? How have they manifested?

cards.title: Releasing the Bind
cards.text:
**Think about how to help your children navigate loyalty conflicts.**

Have you given them explicit permission to like or love your partner? What words have you used?

How might they interpret your relationship as a threat to their deceased parent's place?

What could you say to reassure them that loving your partner is not disloyal?

How is your partner helping or potentially hindering this process?

What ongoing conversations might be needed as this transition continues?
cards.reflection: How can you help release your children from loyalty conflicts?

cards.title: A Permission Conversation
cards.text:
**Have a direct conversation with each child about the loyalty bind.**

**Find a calm, private moment.** Not in passing, but intentionally.

**Name what they might be feeling: "I wonder if you sometimes feel guilty when you have fun with [partner's name], like maybe it means you are forgetting [deceased parent].**"

**Give explicit permission: "I want you to know that it is completely okay to like [partner's name].** That does not take anything away from your [mom/dad]. Your [mom/dad] will always be your [mom/dad]."

Invite their response: "How do you feel about that? Is that something you have been struggling with?"

**This conversation may need to happen more than once.** The loyalty bind is deep. Keep giving permission.

**"The truth will set you free" (John 8:32|Invite their response:).** Speak truth that sets your children free from unnecessary guilt.

When will you have this conversation?
cards.reflection: **Plan when and how you will have a permission conversation with each child.**

activities.title: Building Bridges: Helping Your Children Connect with Your Partner
activities.subtitle: Fostering relationship between your children and future spouse
activities.whyThisMatters: Your children and your partner will become family. Helping them build genuine relationship makes the transition smoother and the family stronger.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Stepparent-child relationships require intentional nurturing and appropriate pacing.

cards.title: Relationship Cannot Be Rushed
cards.text:
**You fell in love with your partner.** Your children did not.

**You have had months or years to develop feelings, build trust, and come to love this person.** Your children are being asked to accept someone you have already come to know deeply.

**This mismatch in relationship timeline is crucial to remember.** Your children need time to develop their own connection with your partner, and that timeline will be different from yours.

**Rushing it backfires.** Forcing togetherness, demanding affection, or moving too fast creates resistance. Children who feel pushed often push back.

**David was so excited for his kids to love his fiancée that he scheduled constant family activities from the start.** His children felt overwhelmed and suffocated. They began resenting both David and his partner for not giving them space to adjust.

**Relationship grows in its own time.** You can create conditions for it, but you cannot force it.

**"There is a time for everything.**.. a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embracing" (Ecclesiastes 3:1|There is a time for everything.**.. a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embracing, 5). There is a time to refrain, to give space, to let relationship develop naturally. Respect that time.

cards.title: Creating Opportunities
cards.text:
**While you cannot rush relationship, you can create opportunities for connection.**

**Shared activities: Find things your children and partner can enjoy together.** Not forced "bonding time" but genuine activities everyone likes.

**Low-pressure time: Being in the same space without agenda.** Casual presence builds familiarity.

**One-on-one time: Your partner spending individual time with each child can build relationship faster than always being in group settings.**

**Shared interests: If your partner and child share an interest, whether sports, music, games, or anything else, nurture that connection.**

**Respecting their world: Your partner showing interest in what matters to your children, attending their events, asking about their lives.**

**Miranda's partner, James, discovered that her daughter loved baking.** He started a tradition of making cookies with her on Saturday mornings. No pressure, just flour and sugar and conversation. That weekly ritual built more relationship than any formal bonding activity could have.

**Create space for connection.** Then step back and let it grow.

**"A friend loves at all times" (Proverbs 17:17|A friend loves at all times).** Your partner is becoming a friend to your children. Friendship grows through shared time and genuine interest.

cards.title: When Connection Is Slow
cards.text:
**Sometimes, despite everyone's best efforts, connection is slow.**

**Your child may be resistant, withdrawn, or openly hostile.** Your partner may feel rejected. You may feel caught in the middle, wanting everyone to just get along.

**This is hard, but it is not necessarily a crisis.** Some children take years to warm up to a stepparent. Slow does not mean never.

What helps:

**Patience without giving up: Keep creating opportunities even when they seem to fail.** Consistency matters.

**Not taking it personally: Your partner cannot personalize your child's resistance.** It is about the situation, not about them as a person.

**Individual work with your child: Understanding what specifically is hard.** Fear? Loyalty? Something about your partner? Address the real issue.

**Professional help if needed: Family counseling can help navigate particularly difficult dynamics.**

**Robert's teenage son was cold to his fiancée for over a year.** They kept showing up, kept being kind, kept not giving up. Slowly, almost imperceptibly, the walls came down. By the time they married, his son had genuinely accepted her. It just took time.

**"Let us not become weary in doing good, for at the proper time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up" (Galatians 6:9|Let us not become weary in doing good, for at the proper time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up).** Do not give up. The harvest may take time, but it can come.

cards.title: Current Relationships
cards.text: How would you describe the current relationship between each of your children and your partner?

cards.title: Building Connection
cards.text:
**Think about how to foster relationship between your children and partner.**

What is working? Where has connection begun to form?

What is not working? Where is there resistance or difficulty?

What shared interests or activities might help build relationship?

Is the pace right? Too fast, too slow, or appropriate?

What does each child specifically need to feel more comfortable?

What role can you play in facilitating without forcing?
cards.reflection: How can you foster genuine relationship between your children and partner?

cards.title: One Connection Opportunity
cards.text:
**Plan one specific opportunity for your children and partner to connect this week.**

**Consider each child's interests.** What would they enjoy that includes your partner?

**Make it low-pressure.** Not a test of whether they bond, just an opportunity to be together.

**Brief your partner.** Make sure they understand the goal is connection, not performance.

**Step back if appropriate.** Sometimes children connect better without you in the middle.

**Notice what happens.** What worked? What did not? What might work better next time?

**"Two are better than one, because they have a good return for their labor" (Ecclesiastes 4:9|Two are better than one, because they have a good return for their labor).** You are building toward a family that works together, supports each other. Every connection opportunity contributes.

What opportunity will you create this week?
cards.reflection: What specific opportunity for connection will you create this week?

activities.title: Their Parent Still Matters: Honoring Memory Through This Transition
activities.subtitle: Keeping the deceased parent's presence alive as your family changes
activities.whyThisMatters: Your children need to know that their deceased parent will not be forgotten or replaced. Intentionally honoring that parent's memory helps children embrace the new without losing the old.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Maintaining connection to the deceased parent supports children's adjustment to new family members.

cards.title: They Fear Being Forgotten
cards.text:
**One of your children's deepest fears is that their parent will be forgotten.**

**As life changes, as new people enter, as time passes, they worry that their mother or father will fade away.** That the family will move on and leave that precious person behind.

**Your remarriage can intensify this fear.** If there is a new wife, does that erase Mom? If there is a new husband, does that replace Dad? If the family looks different, is the old family being erased?

Thirteen-year-old Sophia asked her father through tears: "When you marry Jen, will we still talk about Mom? Will she still be part of our family?" Her father realized his daughter needed explicit reassurance that remarriage would not mean forgetting.

**Your children need to know, clearly and repeatedly, that their deceased parent will always be part of your family's story.** They are not being replaced. They are not being erased. They still matter.

**"The memory of the righteous is a blessing" (Proverbs 10:7|The memory of the righteous is a blessing).** Your children's parent was a blessing. Keep that memory alive as a continued blessing to your family.

cards.title: Intentional Memory Keeping
cards.text:
**Memory does not keep itself.** You have to be intentional about honoring your children's deceased parent through this transition.

**Keep talking about them: Say their name.** Tell stories. Reference their opinions and values. Do not let silence descend around their memory.

**Maintain rituals: If you have established ways of remembering, whether visiting the grave, marking their birthday, or keeping photos displayed, continue them.** Do not let the new relationship displace these practices.

**Include your partner: Let your partner participate in honoring the memory.** They can learn about your late spouse, acknowledge them respectfully, and support your children's ongoing connection.

**Create space for grief: Your children will still have grief that surfaces.** Remarriage does not end their mourning. Make sure they know grief is still welcome in your family.

**William made a point of including his late wife in family conversations even after he remarried.** "Your mom loved sunflowers," he would say when they saw some. His new wife supported this. The children never felt they had to choose between loving their mom's memory and accepting their stepmom.

**"Remember the days of old; consider the generations long past. Ask your father and he will tell you" (Deuteronomy 32:7|he would say when they saw some. His new wife supported this. The children never felt they had to choose between loving their mom's memory and accepting their stepmom. **). Keep telling. Keep remembering. Across the generations.

cards.title: Your Partner's Role in Honoring
cards.text:
**A wise partner will join you in honoring your late spouse rather than competing with their memory.**

**This can be hard.** Your partner may feel insecure, wondering if they can ever measure up, if you still love your late spouse more, if they will always be second.

**But competing with a memory is a losing battle.** The healthy approach is to honor the deceased as someone who was important to the family, someone who shaped the children, someone who deserves respect.

What this looks like:

**Speaking respectfully about the deceased.** Never disparaging them, even in frustration.

**Showing interest in the children's memories.** "Tell me about your mom" rather than changing the subject.

**Supporting memorial practices.** Participating in or encouraging rituals of remembrance.

**Not being threatened by photos, stories, or continued love.** Understanding that the children's love for their parent does not diminish what they might feel for the stepparent.

**Anna was nervous about the shrine of photos her stepchildren had of their mother.** Her husband helped her understand: "Those photos help them feel safe. If you support their connection to their mom, they will eventually be able to connect with you." She chose to honor rather than compete.

**"Honor one another above yourselves" (Romans 12:10|Those photos help them feel safe. If you support their connection to their mom, they will eventually be able to connect with you.).** Your partner honoring your late spouse is a gift to your children.

cards.title: Honoring Their Parent
cards.text: How are you currently honoring your children's deceased parent? What more might be needed?

cards.title: Memory and Transition
cards.text:
**Think about how memory keeping will work through this transition.**

What practices of remembrance are currently in place?

Will any of these need to change with the new marriage? How will you handle that sensitively?

How can your partner participate in honoring your late spouse?

What do your children need to feel secure that their parent will not be forgotten?

How will you make space for ongoing grief alongside the new family formation?
cards.reflection: How will you continue honoring your children's deceased parent through this transition?

cards.title: A Conversation About Memory
cards.text:
**Have a conversation with your children about how their deceased parent will continue to be honored.**

**Reassure them explicitly: "[Parent's name] will always be your [mom/dad].** That never changes. Marrying [partner's name] does not change that."

**Talk about what will continue: "We will still [memorial practices].** We will still talk about [them]. We will still [whatever is meaningful]."

Invite their input: "What would help you feel like [parent] is still part of our family? What is important to you?"

**Include your partner if appropriate: They can express their own commitment to honoring the memory.**

**This conversation provides security.** It tells your children that their parent's place is protected even as the family changes.

**"Only be careful, and watch yourselves closely so that you do not forget the things your eyes have seen" (Deuteronomy 4:9|Only be careful, and watch yourselves closely so that you do not forget the things your eyes have seen).** Help your children not forget. Commit to remembering together.

When will you have this conversation?
cards.reflection: **Plan when and how you will have this conversation about continuing to honor their parent.**

activities.title: Talking It Through: Communication About Your Plans
activities.subtitle: How to discuss your remarriage with your children
activities.whyThisMatters: How you communicate about your plans to remarry matters enormously. Good communication builds trust and helps children feel included rather than blindsided.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Effective communication about major family transitions supports children's adjustment and trust.

cards.title: No Surprises
cards.text:
**Children should not be surprised by major developments in your relationship.**

**They should know you are dating before it becomes serious.** They should know it is becoming serious before you are engaged. They should have time to process each stage before the next one arrives.

**Surprises feel like ambushes.** They leave children feeling that their feelings do not matter, that decisions are being made without them, that they are just expected to go along.

**Brenda announced her engagement at dinner one night, expecting her children to be happy.** Instead, they were shocked and hurt. They had not even known she was dating seriously. The engagement, rather than being celebrated, was received with tears and accusations. She had not given them time to adjust.

**Kids do not get a vote, but they do get a voice.** They need to feel informed, considered, and respected even if they do not control the outcome.

**"Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed" (Proverbs 15:22|Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed).** Bring your children into the conversation. Not to decide for you, but to be heard and considered.

cards.title: Age-Appropriate Information
cards.text:
**What and how you share should match your child's age.**

**Young children need simple, concrete information.** "Mommy has a friend named Tom who she cares about a lot. He is going to be around more. Eventually, he might become part of our family." Reassurance and predictability matter more than details.

**School-age children can handle more explanation.** They need to know how their lives will be affected, whether they will move or change schools or share rooms. They may have many questions. Answer honestly.

**Teenagers need to be treated with more respect for their maturity.** They may have strong opinions. They deserve fuller explanations of your reasoning and genuine engagement with their concerns. Do not dismiss them as "just being teenagers."

**Adult children deserve adult conversation.** They may struggle as much as younger children but need to be approached as adults who have legitimate perspectives.

**Kevin sat down with his sixteen-year-old and talked to her like the young adult she was becoming.** He explained his journey, why he had come to love Marcia, how he had thought carefully about the decision. His daughter did not love it, but she respected being treated maturely.

**"When I was a child, I talked like a child, I thought like a child" (1 Corinthians 13:11|When I was a child, I talked like a child, I thought like a child).** Speak to each child according to their level of understanding.

cards.title: Creating Space for Their Response
cards.text:
**When you share news about your plans, create genuine space for your children's response.**

**Do not demand happiness.** They may not feel happy, and they should not have to pretend.

**Validate their feelings.** "I understand this is a lot to take in. It makes sense that you might have mixed feelings."

**Listen more than you defend.** Resist the urge to immediately counter every concern. First, understand.

**Allow time.** Do not expect instant adjustment. They may need days or weeks to process.

**Keep the door open.** "We can talk about this more whenever you want. I want to know how you are feeling."

**After Jessica told her son about her engagement, he said nothing and went to his room.** She wanted to follow him, to explain, to make him understand. Instead, she gave him space. The next morning, he came to her with questions. He had needed time to process before he could engage.

**"Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak and slow to become angry" (James 1:19|Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak and slow to become angry).** Be quick to listen to your children. Their response matters.

cards.title: Your Communication
cards.text: How have you communicated with your children about your relationship so far? What has gone well and what could improve?

cards.title: Communication Plan
cards.text:
**Think through how you will communicate with your children about your plans.**

What do they already know? What still needs to be communicated?

What is the next major milestone they need to know about?

How will you tell them in a way that is appropriate for their ages?

How will you create space for their responses, even difficult ones?

What ongoing communication do they need as plans progress?
cards.reflection: How will you communicate with your children about your plans going forward?

cards.title: A Communication Check-In
cards.text:
**Have a check-in conversation with your children about how they are feeling about your relationship and plans.**

**Open with an invitation: "I want to know how you are doing with everything that is happening.** Can we talk?"

Ask open questions: "What is going well for you?" "What is hard?" "What questions do you have?" "What worries you?"

**Listen without defending: Take in what they say.** Do not immediately argue or correct.

**Validate: "Thank you for telling me that.** That makes sense." Even if you disagree with their perspective, you can validate their feelings.

**Share what you can: Update them on plans, reassure them about concerns, be honest about what is unknown.**

**Good communication is not a one-time event.** It is an ongoing practice throughout this transition.

**"The tongue of the wise brings healing" (Proverbs 12:18|The tongue of the wise brings healing).** Let your words bring healing, not more wounds.

When will you have this check-in?
cards.reflection: **Plan a check-in conversation with your children about their feelings.**

activities.title: What Will Change: Addressing Practical Concerns
activities.subtitle: Helping children understand how their lives will be affected
activities.whyThisMatters: Children worry about practical changes. Addressing these concerns directly reduces anxiety and helps them feel prepared for the transition.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Concrete information about practical changes reduces children's anxiety about the unknown.

cards.title: The Questions They Wonder About
cards.text:
**Your children have practical questions, even if they do not voice them.**

Will we have to move? Children are attached to their home, their room, their neighborhood. The possibility of moving can be terrifying.

Will I have to change schools? Friends, teachers, routines are all at stake.

Will I have to share my room? Personal space matters intensely, especially to older children.

What will I call this person? The question of names and titles is loaded with meaning.

Will this person be in charge of me? Authority and discipline questions loom large.

Will things be fair? If there are step-siblings, children wonder about fairness in treatment, resources, and attention.

**These questions may seem minor to you, but they are major to your children.** They need answers.

**Twelve-year-old Marcus lay awake at night worrying about whether he would have to share a room with his future stepbrother.** He had never had to share before. The anxiety was eating at him, but he did not know how to ask.

**"The simple believe anything, but the prudent give thought to their steps" (Proverbs 14:15|The simple believe anything, but the prudent give thought to their steps).** Help your children give thought to the steps ahead by giving them information.

cards.title: Providing Answers
cards.text:
**To the extent you know, give your children concrete information about how their lives will change.**

Living situation: Where will everyone live? Whose house? Will there be a move? When?

Rooms and space: Who sleeps where? Will anyone share? What happens to their current room?

School: Any changes to school, transportation, after-school activities?

Rules and routines: Will household rules change? Bedtimes, screen time, chores? Be clear about what stays the same and what might be different.

Relationships: How will your partner interact with them? What authority will they have? What should they call them?

Family activities: How will holidays work? Vacations? Regular family time?

**You may not have all the answers yet.** That is okay. Tell them what you know, what you are still figuring out, and that their input matters.

**Patricia created a family meeting to walk through all the practical changes.** She used a whiteboard to show what was decided, what was still undecided, and what the kids could have input on. The clarity reduced everyone's anxiety.

**"Commit to the Lord whatever you do, and he will establish your plans" (Proverbs 16:3|Commit to the Lord whatever you do, and he will establish your plans).** Make plans and share them. God will establish them.

cards.title: Including Their Voice
cards.text:
**Where possible, include your children in decisions that affect them.**

**You cannot give them veto power over your marriage.** But you can give them voice on matters within the marriage.

Room arrangements: Can they have input on their space? Even choosing paint color gives ownership.

Family rules: Can they participate in creating rules for the new household? This builds buy-in.

Activities: Can they help choose some family activities or traditions?

**Small choices: Even small choices, like what to have at the wedding reception that they would enjoy, make them feel included.**

**Feelings of powerlessness make transitions harder.** When children feel they have some control, some say in their own lives, they cope better.

**Mike asked his kids what they thought about different houses they were considering.** He could not let them decide, but he listened to their input. When they moved, they felt they had been part of the choice, not just dragged along.

**"Listen to advice and accept discipline, and at the end you will be counted among the wise" (Proverbs 19:20|Listen to advice and accept discipline, and at the end you will be counted among the wise).** Listen to your children's advice. You will all be wiser for it.

cards.title: Their Practical Concerns
cards.text: What practical questions do you think your children have? Have you addressed them?

cards.title: Practical Preparation
cards.text:
**Think through the practical changes your children need to understand.**

What changes are certain? Living arrangements, household composition, anything definite.

What is still being decided? Be honest about what you do not know yet.

What questions have your children asked? Have you answered them fully?

What questions have they probably not asked but are wondering about?

Where can they have input? What decisions can include their voice?
cards.reflection: What practical information do your children need? Where can they have input?

cards.title: Address One Practical Concern
cards.text:
**Identify one practical concern and address it this week.**

**Think about what is probably worrying your children most.** The unknown that keeps them up at night.

**If you have an answer, share it clearly.** "I know you have been wondering about [issue]. Here is what is going to happen..."

**If you do not have an answer yet, acknowledge the uncertainty.** "We have not decided about [issue] yet. What are your thoughts? What would you hope for?"

**If they can have input, invite it.** "We are trying to figure out [issue]. What would work best for you?"

**Concrete information reduces anxiety.** Give them what you can.

**"An anxious heart weighs a man down, but a kind word cheers him up" (Proverbs 12:25|If they can have input, invite it.**).** Speak kind, clear words that cheer your children by reducing their anxiety.

What practical concern will you address?
cards.reflection: What one practical concern will you address with your children this week?

activities.title: When It Is Hard: Handling Difficult Responses
activities.subtitle: What to do when children resist, withdraw, or act out
activities.whyThisMatters: Not all children embrace a parent's new relationship. Knowing how to handle resistance, withdrawal, or acting out helps you navigate the hard moments.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Children's difficult responses often reflect underlying grief and fear that need to be addressed.

cards.title: Behavior Is Communication
cards.text:
**When your child acts out, withdraws, or resists, they are communicating something.**

**The teenager who becomes hostile to your partner is saying: "I am scared.** I am grieving. This feels like too much."

**The child who withdraws into silence is saying: "I do not know how to handle this.** I am overwhelmed."

**The young one who suddenly starts misbehaving is saying: "I need attention.** I need to know I still matter."

**Behavior is the language children use when they cannot find words for their feelings.** Before you address the behavior, try to understand what it is communicating.

**When Thomas's daughter started failing classes after he announced his engagement, his first instinct was to punish her.** Then he realized: she was not just being irresponsible. She was drowning in feelings she could not express. The failing grades were a cry for help.

**"A person's wisdom yields patience; it is to one's glory to overlook an offense" (Proverbs 19:11|A person's wisdom yields patience; it is to one's glory to overlook an offense).** Be patient. Look past the behavior to the pain underneath.

cards.title: Responding to Resistance
cards.text:
If your child is openly resistant to your relationship or upcoming marriage:

**Do not dismiss their feelings: "You will get over it" or "You are just being difficult" makes things worse.** Their resistance is real to them.

Seek to understand: What specifically is driving the resistance? Fear? Loyalty? Something about your partner? A need that is not being met?

**Maintain boundaries: Understanding does not mean accepting disrespect.** You can validate feelings while requiring appropriate behavior. "I understand you are upset, and it is not okay to speak to me or to [partner] that way."

**Do not give ultimatums: "Accept this or else" rarely works and can permanently damage your relationship.**

**Keep the relationship primary: Your relationship with your child matters more than their immediate acceptance of your partner.** Prioritize the relationship.

**Karen's son told her he hated her fiancé and would never accept him.** Instead of reacting with anger, she said, "I hear that you are really struggling with this. I love you, and I want to understand. Can you help me understand what is hardest for you?" The conversation that followed was more productive than a fight would have been.

**"A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger" (Proverbs 15:1|I hear that you are really struggling with this. I love you, and I want to understand. Can you help me understand what is hardest for you?).** Respond gently to resistance.

cards.title: When to Get Help
cards.text:
**Sometimes family struggles during this transition require professional help.**

Consider counseling if:

**A child's behavior is extreme or dangerous, whether to themselves or others.**

**Resistance persists despite your best efforts over extended time.**

**Your child is showing signs of depression, anxiety, or other mental health concerns.**

**Family conflict is escalating rather than improving.**

**You feel stuck and do not know what else to try.**

**A family therapist can help everyone communicate better, process underlying grief, and navigate the transition.** This is not failure. It is wisdom.

**Individual therapy for your child may also help.** Having a neutral person to talk to, someone who is not you or your partner, can give them space to process.

**The Rodriguez family entered family therapy after their attempts to blend resulted in constant conflict.** The therapist helped them see patterns they could not see themselves and gave them tools they did not have. The investment in professional help saved their family.

**"Where there is no guidance, a people falls, but in an abundance of counselors there is safety" (Proverbs 11:14|Where there is no guidance, a people falls, but in an abundance of counselors there is safety).** Get professional guidance when you need it.

cards.title: Difficult Responses
cards.text: Have you experienced difficult responses from your children? What has been hardest?

cards.title: Understanding Difficult Behavior
cards.text:
**If your children are having difficult responses, try to understand what is underneath.**

What behaviors have been concerning? Resistance, withdrawal, acting out, other?

What might these behaviors be communicating? Fear, grief, anger, need for attention?

What specific triggers seem to set off difficult behavior?

What have you tried? What has worked and what has not?

Might professional help be beneficial? For your child individually or for the family?
cards.reflection: What might your children's difficult behaviors be communicating? What do they need?

cards.title: Respond to One Difficult Behavior
cards.text:
**If you are experiencing difficult responses from a child, take one step to address it this week.**

**Have a conversation focused on understanding: "I have noticed [behavior].** I want to understand what is going on for you. Can we talk about it?"

**Address an unmet need: If you sense what they need, whether more attention, more reassurance, more information, provide it.**

**Set a boundary with empathy: If behavior has been unacceptable, address it while validating feelings.** "I understand this is hard, and I need you to [expected behavior]."

**Consider professional help: If things are beyond what you can handle, research counselors and make an appointment.**

**Difficult responses are often temporary.** With patience, understanding, and sometimes professional help, most children come through.

**"Be completely humble and gentle; be patient, bearing with one another in love" (Ephesians 4:2|Be completely humble and gentle; be patient, bearing with one another in love).** Bear with your children in love, even when their responses are hard.

What step will you take?
cards.reflection: What step will you take to address difficult responses from your children?

activities.title: Your Partner's Role: Navigating Authority and Relationship
activities.subtitle: Clarifying how your partner will relate to your children
activities.whyThisMatters: Unclear expectations about your partner's role with your children create conflict. Clarifying authority and relationship expectations prevents many problems.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Clear role definition for stepparents supports healthy family functioning.

cards.title: Not a Replacement Parent
cards.text:
**Your partner is not becoming a replacement parent.** They are becoming something else, something that does not have an easy name.

**They will be a parental figure but not the parent.** A caring adult in your child's life but not Mom or Dad. A partner in the household but with different authority than you.

**This ambiguity is inherent in stepparenting.** The role is not clearly defined by society, and each family must figure out what it looks like for them.

**Clarity helps everyone.** When your partner knows their role, when your children know what to expect, when you are all on the same page, there is less conflict and confusion.

**Nathan struggled because he wanted to step into full parental authority immediately.** His stepchildren resented it. "You are not my dad!" was the constant refrain. He had to learn that he was something different, not less important but different.

**"And masters, treat your slaves in the same way.** Do not threaten them, since you know that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven" (Ephesians 6:9|You are not my dad!). Even authority has limits. Your partner's authority with your children will have limits too.

cards.title: Authority Transition
cards.text:
How much authority should your partner have with your children? This evolves over time.

**Early on: Your partner should have minimal direct authority.** You handle discipline and rules. Your partner supports you but does not enforce independently. This prevents the "You are not my parent" battles.

**As relationship builds: Gradually, your partner can take on more authority as trust develops.** Children accept correction better from someone they have relationship with.

**After marriage: Your partner is a full adult in the household and needs to have appropriate authority.** But this authority works best when it has been earned through relationship, not simply assumed.

**Discuss this explicitly with your partner.** Agree on what their role will be at each stage. Communicate it to your children so expectations are clear.

**Rebecca and her fiancé agreed that for the first year after the wedding, she would handle all discipline issues with her kids.** He would support her decisions but not initiate correction. As the kids grew to trust him, they gradually shifted to shared authority. The slow transition prevented many conflicts.

**"The wise in heart are called discerning, and gracious words promote instruction" (Proverbs 16:21|The wise in heart are called discerning, and gracious words promote instruction).** Use discernment in how authority is established. Gracious, gradual promotion of your partner's role works better than forced acceptance.

cards.title: United Front, Different Roles
cards.text:
**You and your partner need to be united while having different roles.**

**United: You agree on values, rules, and expectations.** You support each other. You do not undermine each other in front of the children.

**Different roles: You are the primary parent.** Your partner is the supportive adult. This is not hierarchy for its own sake; it is wisdom about how stepfamily relationships work.

This means:

**Discuss rules and expectations privately.** Present a united front to the children.

**If children try to play you against each other, do not allow it.** "We will discuss this together and let you know."

**Your partner should defer to you on parenting matters, especially early on.** This is not weakness; it is wisdom.

**You support your partner's role.** Do not undermine them in front of the children, even if you disagree with something they did. Discuss it privately later.

**George and his wife had a rule: never disagree about the kids in front of the kids.** If she did something he questioned, he brought it up later, privately. The united front helped the children feel secure even as they adjusted to a new family structure.

**"A house divided against itself will fall" (Luke 11:17|A house divided against itself will fall).** Do not let your house be divided. Unity provides stability.

cards.title: Role Clarity
cards.text: How clear are you and your partner about their role with your children? What questions remain?

cards.title: Defining the Role
cards.text:
**Think through what your partner's role with your children should be.**

What authority will they have initially? After the marriage is established?

How will discipline be handled? Who does what?

How will you present a united front while respecting different roles?

What do your children need to understand about your partner's role?

What conversations do you and your partner need to have to get on the same page?
cards.reflection: What will your partner's role be with your children? How will authority be handled?

cards.title: A Role Conversation
cards.text:
**Have a conversation with your partner about their role with your children.**

Discuss expectations: What do each of you expect regarding their role? Where might you differ?

Agree on authority: What authority will they have when, and how will it evolve?

Discuss discipline: How will rule enforcement be handled? What is your partner's part?

Plan for conflict: What will you do when you disagree? How will you maintain unity?

**If you have already had this conversation, review it.** Has it been working? Does anything need to adjust?

**Clarity between the two of you is the foundation for clarity with your children.**

**"Make plans by seeking advice" (Proverbs 20:18|Make plans by seeking advice).** Seek advice from each other. Make plans together.

When will you have this conversation?
cards.reflection: **Plan a conversation with your partner about their role with your children.**

activities.title: Including Them in the Celebration: Children and Your Wedding
activities.subtitle: Making your children part of the ceremony and celebration
activities.whyThisMatters: Your wedding is not just a union of two people but the formation of a new family. Including your children in meaningful ways honors their place in this new chapter.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Including children in wedding rituals symbolizes their importance and helps them embrace the new family.

cards.title: More Than a Couple's Day
cards.text:
**When you have children, your wedding is not just about you and your partner.** It is about the formation of a new family.

**This does not mean the children are getting married.** But they are entering a new family structure that will shape their lives. Honoring that reality makes the day more meaningful and helps them feel included rather than like spectators to something that happens to them.

**Some children will be excited about the wedding.** Some will have mixed feelings. Some may dread it. Whatever they feel, finding ways to include them acknowledges that this day affects them too.

**Sarah considered eloping to avoid the complexity of a wedding with kids involved.** But she realized that including her children would help them embrace the new family. The wedding became a family event, not just a couple's event, and her children felt honored rather than sidelined.

**"Two are better than one.**.. A cord of three strands is not quickly broken" (Ecclesiastes 4:9|Two are better than one.**.. A cord of three strands is not quickly broken, 12). Your new family is a cord of multiple strands. Let the wedding acknowledge all of them.

cards.title: Ways to Include Children
cards.text:
**There are many ways to include children in your wedding.**

In the ceremony:

**Walking you down the aisle or standing with you at the altar.**

**Participating in a family unity ritual, such as a sand ceremony, candle lighting, or family vows.**

**Doing a reading or prayer.**

**Serving as ring bearer, flower girl, or junior bridesmaid or groomsman, even for older children who can adapt the role.**

**Receiving a ring or gift that symbolizes their place in the new family.**

In the celebration:

**Being part of the wedding party.**

**Giving a toast or being acknowledged in toasts.**

**Having a special dance, parent-child dance extended to include them.**

**Helping with something meaningful, such as the guest book, photos, or music selection.**

**Having friends or activities that make the day fun for them.**

**James had his children stand with him at the altar during the ceremony.** During the vows, his new wife also made promises to the children: to love them, care for them, and be a faithful presence in their lives. The children were not afterthoughts. They were central.

**"A father to the fatherless, a defender of widows, is God in his holy dwelling. God sets the lonely in families" (Psalm 68:5-6|A father to the fatherless, a defender of widows, is God in his holy dwelling.** God sets the lonely in families). God is setting your children in a new family. Let the wedding celebrate that.

cards.title: Respecting Their Feelings
cards.text:
**While including children is important, respect that they may have complicated feelings about the day.**

**Do not force participation.** If a child genuinely does not want to be in the ceremony, do not force them. That creates resentment, not bonding.

**Offer options.** Give them choices about how to participate. Some involvement lets them feel included without demanding more than they can give.

**Acknowledge mixed feelings.** "I know this day might be hard for you as well as happy. It is okay to feel both."

**Have a support person.** Especially for younger children, have a trusted adult assigned to attend to them, someone they can go to if they need a break.

**Plan for their needs.** Make sure the day is not just about adults. Think about what will make it bearable or even enjoyable for them.

**Olivia's teenage daughter wanted nothing to do with the wedding.** Olivia did not force her into the wedding party but found smaller ways to include her: choosing flowers, helping with the playlist, being acknowledged in the ceremony. Her daughter later said she was glad she had not been forced into more but appreciated being included in ways that felt comfortable.

**"Be kind and compassionate to one another" (Ephesians 4:32|Be kind and compassionate to one another).** Be kind and compassionate to your children as you plan this day.

cards.title: Wedding Inclusion
cards.text: How are you planning to include your children in your wedding? What feels right for each child?

cards.title: Planning Their Participation
cards.text:
**Think through how each child can be included in your wedding.**

What would be meaningful for each child? Consider their ages and personalities.

What level of participation would each child be comfortable with?

Are there family rituals you could include in the ceremony?

How can the reception be enjoyable for them, not just for adults?

What support do they need to get through the day?

Are there ways to acknowledge their deceased parent appropriately during the celebration?
cards.reflection: How will you include each child in your wedding in ways that honor their feelings and needs?

cards.title: Talk to Your Children About the Wedding
cards.text:
**Have a conversation with your children about the wedding and their role in it.**

Ask what they want: "How would you like to be part of the wedding? What sounds good to you? What does not?"

**Offer ideas: Share possibilities for their involvement.** Let them respond to options.

**Respect boundaries: If they do not want to do something, accept it graciously.** Find alternatives.

Address concerns: "Is there anything about the wedding that worries you? Anything you want to talk about?"

**Make plans: Once you have agreed on their participation, make it concrete so they know what to expect.**

**This conversation helps them feel like partners in the celebration rather than props in your production.**

**"In everything, do to others what you would have them do to you" (Matthew 7:12|Make plans: Once you have agreed on their participation, make it concrete so they know what to expect. **This conversation helps them feel like partners in the celebration rather than props in your production. ).** Treat your children as you would want to be treated. Include them with respect.

When will you have this conversation?
cards.reflection: **Plan a conversation with your children about their role in the wedding.**

activities.title: The Family Ahead: Preparing for Life After the Wedding
activities.subtitle: Setting your new family up for success
activities.whyThisMatters: The wedding is a beginning, not an ending. Preparing for the daily realities of blended family life sets you up for long-term success.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Intentional preparation for blended family life increases the likelihood of healthy adjustment.

cards.title: The Wedding Is Just the Beginning
cards.text:
**After the wedding comes the life.** And that is where the real work of building a blended family happens.

**The honeymoon period, if there is one, will end.** Daily life will resume. The ongoing work of integrating two families into one will continue for years.

**This is not discouragement.** It is realistic preparation. Families are not built in a day or even a year. Blended families often take three to five years to really feel like a cohesive unit. Knowing this helps you maintain patience and perspective.

**The Hendersons expected everything to click after the wedding.** When it did not, when there was still conflict and adjustment and difficulty, they wondered if something was wrong. A family therapist reassured them: this is normal. Blending takes time.

**"Let us not become weary in doing good, for at the proper time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up" (Galatians 6:9|Let us not become weary in doing good, for at the proper time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up).** You will reap a harvest. But it takes time and persistence. Do not give up.

cards.title: What to Expect
cards.text:
Some realities to expect in your blended family journey:

**Adjustment takes time.** Even with the best preparation, there will be awkwardness, conflict, and learning curves. This is normal.

**Children may regress.** Behavior that had improved may slip after the wedding as children process the finality of the change. Be patient.

**Your marriage needs protection.** The demands of blending can strain your marriage. Prioritize your relationship with your spouse even as you attend to the children.

**Different relationships develop at different speeds.** Your partner may connect quickly with one child and slowly with another. Each relationship has its own timeline.

**The deceased parent remains present.** Grief does not end because you remarried. Your children will continue to miss their parent, and that needs space.

**Extended family complicates things.** Grandparents, aunts, uncles may have opinions about your remarriage that affect your children. Navigate these relationships carefully.

**"Consider it pure joy, my brothers and sisters, whenever you face trials of many kinds, because you know that the testing of your faith produces perseverance" (James 1:2-3|Consider it pure joy, my brothers and sisters, whenever you face trials of many kinds, because you know that the testing of your faith produces perseverance).** Trials produce perseverance. Your blended family journey will produce growth.

cards.title: Setting Up for Success
cards.text:
Some practices that help blended families thrive:

**Maintain your marriage: Regular date time, communication, nurturing your relationship.** Your marriage is the foundation of the family.

**Family meetings: Regular times to check in as a family.** What is working? What is not? Giving everyone a voice.

**One-on-one time: Each parent spending individual time with each child.** This preserves the parent-child bond and helps stepparent-child bonds form.

**Flexibility: Be willing to adjust rules, routines, and expectations as you learn what works.**

**Professional support: Do not hesitate to see a family therapist if needed.** This is not failure; it is wisdom.

**Grace: Extend grace to yourself, your spouse, and your children.** Everyone is doing something hard. Mistakes will happen.

**The Thompson family made family meetings a weekly practice.** Sunday evenings, everyone gathered to share highs and lows, address concerns, and plan the week ahead. It became a cornerstone of their family culture.

**"Above all, love each other deeply, because love covers over a multitude of sins" (1 Peter 4:8|Above all, love each other deeply, because love covers over a multitude of sins).** Love deeply. It will cover the inevitable missteps along the way.

cards.title: Looking Ahead
cards.text:
**Consider what your family will need to thrive after the wedding.**

How will you protect and nurture your marriage amid the demands of parenting?

How will you maintain individual relationships with each child?

What family practices might help build unity, such as meals, meetings, or traditions?

What challenges do you anticipate? How might you address them?

What professional support might be helpful?

What does success look like for your family in one year? Five years?
cards.reflection: What will your family need to thrive? What practices and preparations will help?

cards.title: A Prayer for Your Family
cards.text:
God,

**Thank You for bringing [partner's name] into our lives.** Thank You for the hope of this new family.

**I pray for my children as they navigate this transition.** Give them peace, security, and the ability to open their hearts. Help them grieve what they have lost while embracing what is new.

**Give me wisdom to lead this family well.** Help me balance my children's needs with my marriage. Help me be patient when progress is slow and grateful when breakthroughs come.

**Bless this family we are forming.** Knit us together in love. Make us a place of healing, not more hurt. Let Your presence be the foundation we build on.

**"Unless the Lord builds the house, the builders labor in vain" (Psalm 127:1|Unless the Lord builds the house, the builders labor in vain).** Build this house, Lord. We cannot do it without You.

**In Jesus' name, Amen.**

**Write your own prayer for your family.**
cards.reflection: **Write your prayer for your family as you prepare for this new chapter.**

cards.title: Your Family Commitments
cards.text:
**Make commitments for your family going forward.**

**I commit to putting my children's wellbeing at the center of this transition, even when it is inconvenient.**

**I commit to protecting my marriage as the foundation of our family.**

**I commit to patience, knowing that blending takes years, not months.**

**I commit to maintaining connection with each child individually.**

**I commit to honoring my children's deceased parent as our family grows.**

**I commit to seeking help when we need it.**

**I commit to grace, for myself, my spouse, and my children.**

**I commit to trusting God with this family He is building.**

**Write your commitments in your own words.** Return to them when the journey gets hard.

**Your family is beginning.** May it be blessed.

**"For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans to prosper you and not to harm you, plans to give you hope and a future" (Jeremiah 29:11|For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans to prosper you and not to harm you, plans to give you hope and a future).** He has plans for your family. Good plans. Trust Him.
cards.reflection: **Write your commitments for your family going forward.**
